rows.verified: Employers must manage health and safety risks before people work alone, including risks to contractors and self-employed people working for them.
HSE defines lone workers as people who work by themselves without close or direct supervision.
Lone-working assessments should consider violence, stress and mental health, medical suitability and isolated or rural workplaces.
Some high-risk work needs at least one other person, including specified confined-space, live-electrical, diving, explosives-vehicle and fumigation work.
Employers must train, supervise and monitor lone workers, keep in touch and respond to incidents.
When lone workers visit another employer's workplace, the employer must ask about site risks and control measures.
Supervision levels should be based on the risk assessment; higher-risk work generally needs more supervision.
Monitoring can include agreed contacts, location checks, alarms and return-to-base systems, and these systems and emergency procedures should be tested regularly.
Lone-working risk depends on the task, workplace, isolation, worker competence and health, available supervision, communications and emergency-response arrangements.
HSE lone-working guidance is worker-, task-, site-, supervision-, communication- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level harm probability.
Employers must assess significant risks to workers and implement effective controls, including controls to prevent and manage violence.
Workers and their representatives must be consulted on health and safety risks and controls.
A risk assessment alone does not reduce work-related violence; the actions taken after the assessment are what should reduce risk.
Violence hazards can include verbal abuse, online abuse and physical assault.
Hazards can be identified from worker experience, workplace observation, incident records and known patterns linked to particular work situations.
Risk assessment should consider both the likelihood and seriousness of harm and whether some workers face different or additional risk.
Lone workers may face greater risk because nearby help is absent, while new starters, trainees and other vulnerable workers can also face higher risk.
Employers should consider eliminating the hazard, otherwise control it, record the findings and periodically review the assessment.
Work-related violence risk depends on role, contact with the public, location, lone work, prior incidents, staffing, controls, reporting and response capacity.
HSE violence evidence is workplace-, role-, worker-, control-, incident- and time-specific and is not an exact parcel-level violence probability.
